en: Ah, dear smith Bölökbai—
To see it satisfied the heart.
He cut it from ruby stone
And had sixty facets made
Upon its glass.
When its wheel was turned,
It divided with a shrill sound;
A haze three months away
Appeared as near as three days.
He turned its wheel
And brought it to his true eye.
Toward Chin-Machin and Beijing,
He now aimed the spyglass in earnest:
It was a land pouring forth radiance,
A people renowned as Beijing.
It was fitting that my father Manas
Should challenge it and become its match!
If one faces the numerous people of Beijing,
Their multitude is like black worms.
No mortal has gone against them;
None who faced them remained alive.
He now left Beijing behind
And turned toward Kürpüldök,
Into the hollow of the Sary-Suu,
Toward the face of Kyr-Kaiyng,
To where the clear flowing river
Lies on its western edge.
Kongurbai's countless dark herds,
His myriad livestock taken in tribute,
Seethed like ants;
The accursed one's horses
Could not be distinguished from worms—
They glittered like stars.
Those luckless, barren horses
Resembled growing grass.
Even if all the horses one had heard of and seen
From east to west
Were gathered together,
His horses were more numerous still.
They had settled along the valley;
Khan Kongur's horses
Filled it like spring grass.
One kind among the horses
Was mottled black like a starling.
One kind among the horses
Was pale chestnut with slender tails.
One kind among the horses
Were all alike, tawny-colored,
With white blazes like amulets upon their brows;
All were splendid tulpars.
One kind among the horses
Was red-bay like boils.
The accursed one's horses
Came in countless different kinds.
One kind among the horses
Was dun-gray and dark bay,
Divided into kind after kind.
The accursed one's horses
Appeared different in every color.
Some kinds among the horses
Had black tails and black manes;
Among the horses filling the land,
The bays seemed most numerous.
One breed among the horses
Had bracelet-marked gray animals;
One breed among the horses
Had untamed animals never ridden.
One breed among the horses
Was bright yellow as curds;
One breed among the horses
Gathered in flocks like falcon hoods.
One breed among the horses
Were all matching brown ones;
One breed among the horses
Were all swift brown runners.
The plain of Kürpüldök
Was filled with horses.
One breed among the horses
Were all matching black ones.
The bloodthirsty man blessed with livestock,
That cunning raider of men and horses,
Had one breed among the horses
Appearing white as tents.
Was this not a place to pursue their stallions,
Torment them, and drive them off!
Was this not a place to join the wondrous dust,
Raise a shout,
And raid their horses!
The sight of the horses excited him,
And in his excitement he shouted.
His father's confidant,
His companion destined for the next world.
“Khan Bakai!” he called.
“You who find words in sudden danger,
Who find sight in the darkness,
My lion uncle, come here!
Auspicious when placed before me,
Like a countless host when behind me,
My lion uncle, come here!
My countless army on a journey,
My sure aim when entering a spear fight!
When Khan Bakai rides on patrol,
He is my rugged black mountain.
He feeds the hungry belly,
And restores me when I am worn thin.
Uncle Bakai, my elder,
Did you see what I saw?
Did you learn what I learned?
Seething and writhing like worms,
His horses fill the land.
The men who guard those horses
Seem to number nine hundred.
He has livestock of every kind,
And among his horses
There are tulpars too.
The vast herd has no discernible pattern;
Among those horses,
What is there, and what is not?
Is this not a place to bring
Merciless turmoil?!
Is this not a place to raise a battle cry
And level the spear?!
Is this not a place to drive off the horses
With cries ringing out?!
Is this not a place to clear away the herdsmen
And slaughter them utterly!”
When Semetey said this,
Lion Bakai answered:
“My dear only one,
The infidels are as numerous as ants,
And hero Kongurbai is a great warrior.
Against infidels like black worms,
Even the strongest cannot prevail
In fighting hero Khan Kongurbai!
Come with fierce wrath,
And come heeding your uncle's words!
The Chinese people beyond the ridge—
If they surge forth, they are a flowing flood.
One cannot match them in battle,
Nor overcome them in wrestling.
The reason they will not come is this:
From the squared pass and cliff,
We alone have emerged from the nest.
Parted from their horses,
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
Your boys, remained back there.
You have no pass on which to set your resolve,
No place where you lie entrenched!
We revealed our sluggishness;
We let Muradyl, son of Kyrym,
Raid the horses from among us,
And left with the baggage train
The hero who was our support at the waist.
If we grapple back and forth
With the accursed Chinese people,
There is no army to give us support.
In my old age, I, Bakai,
Have none of the people I longed to bring;
I no longer have my former power
To stand and fight without fleeing.
I have no strength to do battle;
My foal, I have no means
To serve as your support.
I was keen, but I have grown weary;
Parted from my twin, lion Manas,
Parted from my match,
My noble one gone, I have aged.
I was sharp steel, but I am chipped;
This wretched life has passed,
How have I now become so feeble?
When I possessed perfect strength,
When my courage was abundant,
With my leather warrior's belt girded at my waist,
If seventy thousand troops came,
I would enter lightly clad and attack,
Would I not stand firm upon the pass and road!
When I possessed my dear strength,
Clad and girded in bulletproof armor,
If one hundred twenty thousand enemies appeared,
I would enter alone among the host and attack;
Would I not stand firm—was I ever absent?!
Joy and suffering, side by side,
It was the time they accompanied me;
The accursed, barren world
Made sport of Bakai
And deceived him.
With my beard grown white,
I have come on campaign, my foal,
In this very year when I am ready to die.
My accursed joints wobble,
My accursed eyes merely glimmer.
I have no teeth to chew food;
It is Bakai's time to die,
My precious son, I have no strength.
I have become your traveling companion,
But have no power to clash in battle;
If the black Chinese below
Suddenly surge over us,
I have no means to support you!
Would that a horse never tired after six months' riding;
Would that a horse never grew old.
Until this dear head entered the grave,
Would that a hero never grew old.
Old age is humiliation;
Rather than live on, aged and unable to die,
It would be better to be dead.
From the road I reconnoitered at night,
Traveling by day, I lost my way.
It seems I have beheld
The oppression of judgment;
This accursed, barren world—
While sitting fully alive,
It seems I have died!
My son, unwillingly abandon hope
Of your support, uncle Bakai!
If my Allah sets your work right,
If the spirit of Manas,
Who departed for the next world, is close at hand,
You shall bring turmoil in due order
And raid the horses
Of the Kalcha whose tumult is unlike any other's!
There in the hollow of the flowing river,
Along the Sary-Suu,
There is a tent with golden poles;
Inside that tent
Is the infidel Karagul.
That swine Karagul
Has a cunning beyond that of mortals.
That accursed Karagul—
Here is the dark hour!
Broad-jawed and flat-tongued,
A great orator who never stumbles,
If you let him deceive you, my foal,
The time of a brave man will be lost.
The stratagems of Karagul
Are inferior to none.
That is the accursed man himself;
Do not let him deceive you, my foal,
For he is the eye of calamity!
Watch carefully, my only one;
He is the true enemy himself!
An eloquent and skillful slave,
May his wish never be fulfilled,
A mighty slave, the best among the Chinese.
His speech is like honey and sugar;
He has twice deceived
Not only you, but your uncle Bakai.
Keen-eyed, a judge of warriors—
That is the accursed man himself.
Karagul, doomed to die in flames,
That is the crooked slave himself.
He is the khan of the horse herders;
His wrath is complete, though he is an infidel,
And the cunning of Karagul
Is second to none.
May Karagul, doomed to die in flames,
